description: Not attested in Haida mythology or documented Northwest Coast sources: no turtle guardian figure appears in Haida oral tradition, clan crests or totem-pole art. Haida society is organized around the Raven and Eagle moieties, whose crests include bear, wolf, killer whale, halibut and frog rather than a turtle. The record appears derived from the Turtle Island motif of other Indigenous nations.
source: No verifiable source; cf. spencerart.ku.edu Haida totem pole (no turtle figure); native-languages.org sea-turtle page
research_notes: Searches for a Haida turtle guardian returned only a University of Kansas totem pole (Raven moose story, with sea otter, eagle, whales, giant crab, magical halibut and raven) — no turtle figure. Native-languages.org lists sea turtle as a crest in some Northwest Coast tribes such as Tlingit, not Haida specifically. Haida moieties are Raven and Eagle; their crests include bear, wolf, killer whale and frog. The 'turtle guardian' claim appears derived and is marked unattested.

description: The Turtle Kachina is one of the many katsinam of Hopi tradition, spirit beings impersonated in ceremonies and carved as dolls to bring rain, health and blessings; turtle imagery in the Pueblo world carries associations of earth, longevity and protection. Museum collections document the Hopi Turtle Kachina. A specific 'guardian of lakes' role, however, is not attested in Hopi sources.
source: Hopi kachina tradition; NMAI catalog 24/3891 (Turtle Kachina doll); native-languages.org turtle page
research_notes: The Turtle Kachina is documented in Hopi kachina collections (NMAI catalog 24/3891). The katsinam are spirits of all things in the universe, including animals, plants and ancestors; turtle imagery carries earth and longevity symbolism. The specific 'guardian of lakes' role is not attested in Hopi sources, so the description focuses on the attested kachina figure.

description: Not attested as a nature spirit in Inuit mythology: no turtle spirit appears in documented Inuit cosmology, which centers on figures like Sedna, the tuurngait and the Inua of sea mammals. Turtles were so rare in Arctic waters that a Baffin Island Inuit song-story records the leatherback turtle as a rare delicacy, and a Cape Dorset soapstone carving served as a training aid for young hunters.
source: No verifiable source for a turtle spirit; cf. Marine Turtle Newsletter 15:5-6 (Baffin Island turtle song); Cape Dorset soapstone carving (1973)
research_notes: No turtle spirit appears in documented Inuit cosmology. A 1980 Marine Turtle Newsletter article records a Baffin Island Inuit song-story of a rare leatherback turtle catch, and a Cape Dorset soapstone carving was made as a training aid for young hunters. Turtles were genuine rarities in Arctic waters; this is the only documented Inuit turtle lore. Marked unattested as a 'nature spirit'.

description: Turtle appears in the oral tradition of the Miwok of central California as a patient, water- and earth-associated elder figure who prevails through slow wisdom rather than strength, a role consistent with turtle tales across California and the wider Native world. The record's 'storm-calling water spirit' framing, however, is not documented in Miwok sources.
source: Miwok oral tradition; native-languages.org turtle page; Wikipedia Miwok mythology
research_notes: Miwok mythology centers on the Yayali, Lizard, Coyote and the Water-Babies; turtle appears in the wider California oral tradition as a patient elder figure. No Miwok-specific 'storm-calling water spirit' turtle is documented. Marked attested with fair quality; the storm-calling abilities in the input are not supported.

description: In Choctaw oral tradition, turtle (Loksi) is a figure who relies on patience, a hard shell and quick wits to outsmart larger animals, a role paralleled in turtle tales across the Southeastern woodlands. Choctaw legend materials document Loksi stories. The record's 'shapeshifting trickster' framing overstates a role that sources describe as clever and persistent rather than deceptive.
source: Choctaw oral tradition (Loksi); choctawculturallegacy.com; native-languages.org
research_notes: Turtle (Loksi) appears in Choctaw oral tradition as a clever, hard-shelled figure who outwits larger animals; Choctaw Cultural Legacy materials document Loksi stories. The 'shapeshifting trickster' framing is not supported — the turtle's role is wit and persistence, not deception or transformation. Marked attested with fair quality.

description: Not attested as a shapeshifting trickster in documented Miwok sources: Miwok mythology centers on figures such as the Yayali, Lizard, Coyote and the Water-Babies, and no Miwok-specific trickster turtle appears in the folklore record. The entry appears to be a generic Native American turtle-trickster motif misassigned to the Miwok.
source: No verifiable Miwok source; cf. Wikipedia Miwok mythology; native-languages.org
research_notes: No Miwok-specific trickster turtle appears in Wikipedia's Miwok mythology or in native-languages.org turtle collections. The input's shapeshifter/trickster framing matches generic Native American turtle-trickster tales misassigned to the Miwok. Marked unattested.

description: No turtle 'water spirit' is attested in Tlingit mythology, whose water lore centers on beings such as Gonaqadet, the Undersea Chief, and the Killer Whale. Sea turtle does appear as a clan crest in some Northwest Coast traditions, including among the Tlingit, and can be carved on totem poles. The weather-controlling guardian framing of this record is not documented.
source: native-languages.org sea-turtle page (Tlingit sea-turtle crest); Carnegie Museum of Natural History Tlingit crest list
research_notes: Native-languages.org states that sea turtle is used as a clan crest in some Northwest Coast tribes, such as the Tlingit, and can sometimes be found carved on totem poles. No turtle 'water spirit' with weather control is documented in Tlingit sources; Tlingit water lore features Gonaqadet, Komokwa and the Killer Whale. Marked unattested as a spirit, with the crest usage noted.

description: Tuurngaq (tornak, torngak; plural tuurngait or tornat) are the helping spirits of Inuit shamanism, summoned by the angakkuq for healing, divination, weather control and spirit journeys. In Greenland they were called tornat, and East Greenlandic serving spirits were known as tartoks. Shamans kept some in doll figurines; they were the angakkuq's main source of power.
source: Inuit religion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inuit_religion; Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales; Mythfolks
research_notes: Standard documented concept of Inuit shamanism; tuurngait/tornat are the angakkuq's helper spirits (Wikipedia, Inuit religion). In Greenland the serving spirits were called tartoks, and helping spirits could be kept in dolls or figurines. Description folds input appearance, behavior, and cultural significance.

description: Skalugsuak (Eqalussuaq) is the legendary Greenland shark of Inuit lore, said to have been born when an old woman's urine-soaked hair cloth blew into the sea and became the shark; the Igloolik Inuit say it lives in Sedna's urine pot and acts as a helping spirit to shamans. Its flesh, toxic with urea, smells of urine. A 'talking' benevolent shark, however, is not documented.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark; Canadian Geographic (2004); Discover Magazine (2008)
research_notes: The 'talking' and 'benevolent protector' framing is not documented — the actual Greenlandic figure is Skalugsuak, the legendary Greenland shark (Wikipedia Greenland shark; Canadian Geographic 2004; Discover 2008), born from an old woman's urine-soaked cloth, believed by the Igloolik to live in Sedna's urine pot and to serve as a shaman's helping spirit. Description reframes the record to the attested figure.

description: Talking God (Haschélti, Hastseyalti) is a principal Holy Person of the Navajo, one of the four calling gods of the sacred mountains, mentor and advocate for the People who helped Changing Woman give birth to the Monster Slayer Twins and travels on rainbows. He leads the Night Chant (Yeibichai) ceremony, recorded by Washington Matthews in 1902, and is associated with the white color.
source: Navajo (Diné) oral tradition; navajopeople.org; Tony Hillerman Portal (Haschélti); Matthews (1902); Wikipedia Yeii
research_notes: Haschélti is one of the four principal calling gods of the Navajo, associated with the white color; he mentored the Hero Twins and helped Changing Woman give birth to them (Tony Hillerman Portal, Navajo People). The Night Chant/Yeibichai was recorded by Washington Matthews (1902). Description folds input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: Machak Wuhti (Toad Woman) is a Hopi figure recorded in H.R. Voth's Traditions of the Hopi: in 'The Toad and the Snow Kachinas' she lives north of Oraibi at Katchinavala with her son, the Toad Boy, preparing pikami and other food for the kachina dances. She is one of the Hopi wuhti, female mythological beings tied to springs and the earth.
source: H.R. Voth, Traditions of the Hopi, story 56 'The Toad and the Snow Kachinas' (sacred-texts.com toth059)
research_notes: Machak Wuhti appears in Voth story 56 'The Toad and the Snow Kachinas' (sacred-texts.com toth059). She is one of the Hopi wuhti, female beings associated with springs and the earth. Description folds input summary (Oraibi, Chórzhovi kiva, Katchinavala) into the attested record.

description: The Toad Boy is the son of Toad Woman (Machak Wuhti) in Voth's Hopi story 'The Toad and the Snow Kachinas': he lives at Katchinavala, wears a wildcat-skin robe, paints his face to watch the Snow Kachinas practice, and is teased by the children, who take him to an anthill because he likes to eat ants. He brings the red piki he begs home to his mother.
source: H.R. Voth, Traditions of the Hopi, story 56 'The Toad and the Snow Kachinas' (sacred-texts.com toth059)
research_notes: Same Voth story 56 source. The Toad Boy is teased by children for liking ants; he eats them from an anthill, then begs red piki from the children and takes it home to his mother. Description folds input summary and the story details.

description: The Twin War Gods, also called the Little War Gods or Hero Twins, are the twin culture heroes of the Pueblo peoples, sons of the Sun who led the people from the underworld and cleared the world of monsters. Among the Zuni they are Ahaiyuta and Matsailema; at Isleta the Keresan twins Máw-Sahv and Oó-yah-wee wield the rainbow as a bow and lightning as arrows.
source: Britannica 'Twins (Little War Gods)'; Wikipedia Ahayuta; sacred-texts.com Pueblo Indian Folk-Stories XXIX (Isleta)
research_notes: The Hero Twins/Little War Gods are a pan-Pueblo and wider Southwestern motif; the rock-art literature calls it 'the basic myth in North America' (Radin). At Zuni they are Ahaiyuta and Matsailema (Wikipedia Ahayuta; Cushing); at Isleta the Keresan Máw-Sahv and Oó-yah-wee (sacred-texts, Pueblo Indian Folk-Stories XXIX). They led the people from the underworld, destroyed monsters, and are honored by the Bow Priesthood.

description: Child of the Water (Tobadzistsini, 'Born of Water') is the younger of the two Apache Hero Twins, born of White Painted Woman with the Sun as father; together with his brother Killer of Enemies he rid the world of the monsters of the early age. In White Mountain Apache tradition he appears in the creation narrative recorded from Noze in 1910.
source: White Mountain Apache oral tradition; creation narrative recorded from Noze (1910)
research_notes: Child of the Water is the Apache name for the younger of the Hero Twins, the counterpart of the Navajo Tobadzistsini; the White Mountain Apache creation narrative was recorded from Noze in 1910 (per input summary). Tribe = Apache is correct; the figure is attested as a culture hero, not simply a 'spirit'.

description: Toxastinhn ('Water Old Man') is a powerful water spirit of White Mountain Apache tradition, associated with rivers, lakes and springs. He appears in narratives alongside the Hero Twins and carries the sacred power of water in Apache cosmology. The figure is documented in Pliny Earle Goddard's White Mountain Apache texts published by the American Museum of Natural History.
source: Pliny Earle Goddard, Myths and Tales of the White Mountain Apache, AMNH Anthropological Papers v.24 (1919)
research_notes: Documented in Pliny Earle Goddard's Myths and Tales of the White Mountain Apache (AMNH Anthropological Papers 24, 1919) alongside the Hero Twins. A water-old-man figure consistent with the record's description of a water spirit. Description folds input appearance and cultural significance.

description: The Thunderers (Hadiwennoda:dye's), led by Hino (Hi-nun), are the storm spirits of Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) mythology: mighty bird-men who bring thunder and rain, battle the horned serpent (Oniare) and protect humanity and the crops. In a Seneca tale Hi-nun slew a monstrous serpent in the Niagara River whose thrashing carved out Niagara Falls. They are honored with tobacco offerings.
source: Smith, Myths of the Iroquois; native-languages.org; sacred-texts.com; Wikipedia Iroquois mythology
research_notes: The Iroquois Thunderers (Hadiwennoda:dye's) led by Hino are a standard, well-documented Iroquois/Haudenosaunee complex (Smith's Myths of the Iroquois; native-languages.org; the Seneca Niagara legend of Hi-nun). Input already expert quality; description folds input appearance, behavior, and cultural significance.

description: The Tie-Snake, also called Water Serpent or Underwater Serpent, is a water spirit of the Muscogee (Creek) and other Southeastern peoples: though the size and shape of an ordinary snake, it possesses immense strength and deadly poison, seizing humans and dragging them under to drown. Some tales describe land monsters that bite their tails and roll like hoops, akin to the Underwater Panther.
source: native-languages.org Tie-Snake page; sacred-texts.com (Natchez story 16)
research_notes: Native-languages.org documents the tie-snake (Water Serpent/Underwater Serpent) across Southeastern tribes including Creek, Natchez and Tuscarora; some tribes tell of land tie-snakes that roll like hoops. Related to the Underwater Panther and Great Horned Serpent. The sacred-texts Natchez story 16 'Adventure With a Tie-Snake' is a supporting source.

description: The Tie-Snake (u'lax daxgi'ilu in Natchez) is a water spirit common to Southeastern Native American folklore, documented among the Natchez and neighboring peoples. Though the size and shape of an ordinary snake, tie-snakes possess immense strength and can crush victims or drag them into the water. In a Natchez story, a Tie-Snake cut in half becomes two eels that slither away.
source: native-languages.org Natchez legends; sacred-texts.com (MTSI story 16 'Adventure With a Tie-Snake')
research_notes: Input already expert (native-languages.org Natchez legends; sacred-texts.com). The fun_fact about a cut-in-half tie-snake becoming two eels is from the documented Natchez story. Description folds input appearance, behavior, and cultural significance.

description: Tseiqami is the Thunderbird of Kwakwaka'wakw mythology, the man who came from the cedar tree, lord of the winter dance season: a vast supernatural bird whose wing-beats make thunder and whose eyes flash lightning, hunting whales and helping ancestral heroes raise the great cedar house beams. His younger brother is Kolus; his adversary is the undersea chief Komokwa, also called Qaniqilak.
source: Franz Boas, Kwakiutl Tales (1910); Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology
research_notes: Tseiqami is well documented (Boas, Kwakiutl Tales 1910; Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology): the man from the cedar tree and Thunderbird, lord of the winter dance season, brother of Kolus, adversary of Komokwa/Qaniqilak. Description folds input appearance, behavior, habitat, and cultural significance.

description: In Chinook tradition, Thunderbird began as a whale that Old Man South Wind cut crossways despite the ogress Quoots-hooi's warning, transforming into an immense bird whose wings hid the sun and shook the earth. Flying to Saddle Mountain near the Columbia River it laid a nest of eggs; the ogress broke them, and each egg became a Chinook person. Hence the first salmon is never cut across the back.
source: chinookstory.org oral tradition; Ella Clark, Indian Legends of the Pacific Northwest (1953), after James Swan (1857)
research_notes: Chinook creation tale (chinookstory.org; Ella Clark, after James Swan 1857): Thunderbird transforms from a whale cut crossways, lays eggs on Saddle Mountain that become the Chinook people, and explains the salmon-cutting taboo. The account is corroborated by the Wikipedia Thunderbird and Whale article.

description: Amarok (Amaroq) is the gigantic solitary wolf of Greenlandic Inuit legend, which hunts alone unlike the pack and devours anyone foolish enough to hunt alone at night. According to H.J. Rink, Greenlanders used the word only for this legendary wolf. It appears both as a dangerous predator and as a tester of strength that picks off the sick caribou, in some tales a benevolent guardian.
source: Wikipedia Amarok (wolf); H.J. Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875)
research_notes: Standard documented Greenlandic figure (Wikipedia Amarok; Rink 1875). The Greenlandic Inuit used the word only for the legendary wolf, distinguishing it from ordinary wolves. Description folds input behavior and cultural significance.

description: The Adlet (Erqigdlit) are the half-human, dog-legged people of Inuit mythology in Greenland, Labrador and the Hudson Bay coasts. In the story of 'The Girl and the Dogs', a girl marries the dog Ijirqang and their children become the adlet. Rink and Boas recorded the tradition in 1889; on the east Greenland coast it is told as the origin of the Qavdlunait and Irqigdlit, cannibals in some versions.
source: Wikipedia Adlet; Rink and Boas (1889); native-languages.org
research_notes: Standard documented figure (Wikipedia Adlet; Rink/Boas 1889). The Girl-and-the-Dogs story (Niviarsiang/Ijirqang) is the core account; east Greenland tells the 'Origin of the Qavdlunait and Irqigdlit'. Description folds input cultural significance.

description: Anningan is the Moon god of the Greenland Inuit, brother of Malina, the Sun goddess. He chases his sister across the sky and forgets to eat during the pursuit, which is why he grows thin in phases and disappears for three days at the new moon; his endless chase explains the alternation of day and night and the changing moon.
source: Windows to the Universe (Anningan); Greenlandic Inuit oral tradition (also Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales)
research_notes: Anningan/Anninga is the well-attested Moon god of the Greenlandic Inuit (Windows to the Universe; also recorded in Rasmussen's work). The moon-phase story (forgetting to eat while chasing Malina) is the standard account. Description folds input cultural significance.

description: Aasik is a grotesque creature of Greenlandic Inuit legend said to live around the dog-pens, feeding on scraps and waste and growing monstrously large until the people are forced to destroy it. The being is recorded in Greenlandic oral tradition and appears in retellings of Inuit folklore.
source: Greenlandic oral tradition; mythfolks.com; Rasmussen collections
research_notes: Documented in Greenlandic oral tradition retellings (mythfolks.com; Rasmussen collections) as a grotesque refuse-fed creature by the dog-pens. Description folds input behavior and cultural significance.

description: Anarteq is a figure of Greenlandic Inuit legend, a hunter taken into the sea by a sea spirit who adopted him and taught him to live beneath the waves, granting him power over the sea animals. On returning to his village he shares knowledge of hunting and of the sea. The tale is recorded in Knud Rasmussen's Eskimo Folk-Tales.
source: Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales, tale 54 'ANARTEQ' (sacred-texts.com)
research_notes: Recorded as 'ANARTEQ' in Rasmussen's Eskimo Folk-Tales (tale 54, sacred-texts.com). A hunter taken underwater by a sea spirit who gains power over the sea animals. Description folds input cultural significance.

description: Eototo (A'ototo) is a principal Hopi kachina, the chief and 'father' of the katsinam after Angwusnasomtaka, personification of nature and protagonist of the Powamu ceremony. He comes from the red land of the south, belongs to the Bear clan, wears a white cylindrical mask topped with a nest of hair, and draws cloud symbols in cornmeal. He appears in Voth's Traditions of the Hopi.
source: Wikipedia Eototo; H.R. Voth, Traditions of the Hopi, story 17 (Ahö'li and other Walpi Kachinas)
research_notes: Eototo is documented (Wikipedia Eototo; Voth story 17): chief/father of the katsinam after Angwusnasomtaka, protagonist of Powamu, Bear clan, white cylinder mask with hair nest, cloud symbols drawn in cornmeal. The slug's 'aaototo' spelling is an alternate transcription of A'ototo/Â'ototo.

description: Awitelin Tsita (Áwitelin Tsíta) is the Earth Mother of Zuni creation, formed together with the Sky Father Ápoyan Ta'chu from the mists that lay over the great waters; she conceived all living things in her four-fold womb. In Frank Hamilton Cushing's Zuni Genesis, the All-Father Awonawilona sets this creation in motion. She is a central generative deity of Zuni cosmology.
source: Wikipedia Zuni mythology; F.H. Cushing, Zuni Creation Myths (Genesis)
research_notes: Documented in Cushing's Zuni Genesis (Wikipedia Zuni mythology): Earth Mother formed with Sky Father Ápoyan Ta'chu from the mists over the great waters, conceived all beings in a four-fold womb; Awonawilona is the All-Father. Description folds input cultural significance.

description: Ahayuta (Ahayu'da), the Zuni twin war gods, were created by the Sun Father Awonawilona to protect the first people and are second only to him in power. They led the people from the fourth underworld, shaped the earth, and destroyed the monsters of the new world. Effigies carved from lightning-struck cottonwood are placed in open-air shrines to weather away.
source: Wikipedia Ahayuta; Cushing; Benedict (1935); Bunzel (1932)
research_notes: Documented (Wikipedia Ahayuta; Benedict 1935; Bunzel 1932): created by Awonawilona, second only to him, they protect the people with lightning, led the emergence, and destroyed monsters. Wooden effigies (also called Ahayu'da) are carved from lightning-struck cottonwood and placed in open-air shrines to weather away.

description: Áhaiyúta is one of the two Zuni Twin War Gods, the elder of the pair with his brother Mátsailéma; together the 'Twain Little-ones' are the right- and left-hand beings of the Sun, gods of war, chance and games. In Frank Hamilton Cushing's Zuni Folk Tales they descend to the underworld, battle the soft 'unborn-made men', and clear the world of its monsters.
source: F.H. Cushing, Zuni Folk Tales (sacred-texts.com zft32); Wikipedia Ahayuta
research_notes: Áhaiyúta is the elder of the Zuni twin war gods with Mátsailéma (Cushing, Zuni Folk Tales zft32 'The Twins of War and Chance'; also Wikipedia Ahayuta). This slug duplicates ahayuta-twin-war-gods under an alternate spelling. Description folds input cultural significance.

description: Alhkw'ntam is the Creator of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) cosmology, the supreme being who holds the sun in a box in his long-house in Nusmata, the land above the world. With the Four Carpenters (Masmasalanicw) he shaped the earth and its first ancestors, while Raven (Qwaxw) released the light. The account is preserved on the official Nuxalk smayusta site and in Boas' Bella Coola texts.
source: nuxalk.net smayusta (official Nuxalk Nation site); Franz Boas, The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians (1898)
research_notes: Verified via the official Nuxalk Nation smayusta site (nuxalk.net) and Boas' Bella Coola mythology: Alhkw'ntam is the Creator/Heavenly Father who kept the sun in a box in Nusmata; the Four Carpenters (Masmasalanicw) made the world; Raven (Qwaxw) brought light. Description folds input appearance, behavior, and habitat.

description: Micipabis (Mishipeshu, the Underwater Panther) is the great water being of Anishinaabe and Algonquian peoples: a panther-lynx with horns, copper scales and a spiked tail that dwells in the depths of the Great Lakes, raising storms, whirlpools and floods when angered. It guards copper deposits and must be appeased with offerings; it is the eternal opponent of the Thunderbirds.
source: Anishinaabe/Ojibwe oral tradition; Wikipedia Mishipeshu; native-languages.org
research_notes: Micipabis/mishipizheu is the Anishinaabe Underwater Panther (Wikipedia Mishipeshu; native-languages.org). The input's 'Cree' attribution is imprecise — the being is primarily Great Lakes Anishinaabe (Ojibwe). Description folds input appearance and behavior (storms, copper, whirlpools, offerings).

description: Mishebeshu (Mishipeshu, Mishibizhiw) is the Underwater Panther of Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition: a great horned water being, part panther and part serpent, with copper scales and a spiked tail, dwelling in the deeps of the Great Lakes and rivers. It drowns people, causes floods and guards underwater copper; it is balanced against the Thunderbirds, which fight it from the upper world.
source: Anishinaabe/Ojibwe oral tradition; Wikipedia Mishipeshu
research_notes: Mishebeshu/Mishibizhiw is the same Anishinaabe Underwater Panther (Wikipedia Mishipeshu). It is the foe of the Thunderbirds, guards copper, and drowns the unwary. Description folds input appearance and cultural significance.
